sentences.label: Lowering the risk
sentences.text: These add up independently, and these lower the risk: being a woman takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 15% to about 1% and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 4%; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 20% at 118 to about 13% at 175 beats per minute; and through this sum alone, compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina or non-anginal chest pain lowers it to about 2% and atypical angina to about 7%, and chest pain brought on by exercise lowers it to about 11%.

sentences.label: Raising the risk
sentences.text: Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 15% at 0 to about 95% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher; a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it to about 41%, and higher cholesterol raises it steadily, from about 8% at 193 mg/dL to about 34% at 308 mg/dL.

Through this sum alone, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 55%, and more ST depression on exercise (from about 13% at 0 mm to about 21% at 2.8 mm) and older age (from about 11% at 42 to about 19% at 66 years) raise it steadily; chest pain type, chest pain on exercise, the ST segment, ST depression and age also act through the parts below.

sentences.label: Rare results
sentences.text: Some rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 and 17): a thallium result coded 4 raises the risk to about 95%, and through this sum alone a downsloping ST segment lowers it to about 13%; the model ignores the resting ECG.

This part reads chest pain type, resting blood pressure, chest pain on exercise, ST depression on exercise and the slope of the ST segment; for the typical patient, whose ST segment slopes up, it changes little: through it, typical angina and chest pain on exercise each leave the predicted risk at about 15%.

Its effect shows for patients whose ST segment does not slope up: across the whole model, more ST depression raises their risk in an uneven way, from about 51% at 0 mm to about 85% at 2.8 mm, against about 13% to about 21% with an upsloping ST segment.
Higher resting blood pressure raises the risk in an uneven way only for them, from about 55% at 110 mm Hg to about 77% at 155 mm Hg, while with an upsloping ST segment it stays at about 15%.
More ST depression also counts more without typical angina (from about 13% to about 21%, against about 2% to about 4% with it), rising in an uneven way.

This part reads age, chest pain type and chest pain on exercise and acts on 132 of 242 training patients, 83 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 99% without it and about 98% with it.

Through it, older age changes nothing until about 60 years (between 54 and 60 years for different patients), then lowers the predicted risk steadily: for a typical patient from about 17% at 42 to about 8% at 66 years.
Across the whole model, older age raises the risk steadily when exercise brings on chest pain (from about 9% to about 16%), but lowers it when it does not (from about 12% to about 10%).
Through it, any chest pain type other than no chest pain symptoms raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 15% to about 24%, and chest pain on exercise to about 18%.

lead.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results) the model predicts a risk of heart disease of about 15%; it adds up most of its inputs independently, one part adds ST depression and resting blood pressure in an uneven way for patients whose ST segment does not slope up, and a second part acts on 132 of 242 training patients through age, chest pain type and chest pain on exercise.

evidence.text: For the typical patient, whose ST segment slopes up, it changes little: through it, typical angina and chest pain on exercise each leave the predicted risk at about 15%.

Across the whole model, more ST depression raises the risk in an uneven way, from about 51% at 0 mm to about 85% at 2.8 mm when the ST segment does not slope up, against about 13% to about 21% when it does.
Higher resting blood pressure raises it in an uneven way from about 55% at 110 mm Hg to about 77% at 155 mm Hg when the ST segment does not slope up, and leaves it at about 15% when it does.
More ST depression counts more without typical angina (from about 13% to about 21%, against about 2% to about 4% with it), rising in an uneven way.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 242 training patients.

hypothesis.text: This part raises the predicted risk in an uneven way with ST depression on exercise and resting blood pressure for patients whose ST segment does not slope up, and changes little for patients whose ST segment slopes up.

evidence.text: It acts on 132 of 242 training patients, 83 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 99% without it and about 98% with it.

Through it, older age changes nothing until about 60 years (between 54 and 60 years for different patients), then lowers the risk steadily: for a typical patient from about 17% at 42 to about 8% at 66 years.
Across the whole model, older age raises the risk steadily when exercise brings on chest pain (from about 9% to about 16%), but lowers it when it does not (from about 12% to about 10%).
Through it, any chest pain type other than no chest pain symptoms raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 15% to about 24%, and chest pain on exercise to about 18%.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 242 training patients.

hypothesis.text: This part lowers the predicted risk for older patients: through it, age changes nothing until about 60 years, then lowers the risk steadily, for patients without chest pain on exercise.

evidence.text: It is made up of the inputs that feed the score directly and two parts, the exertional ischaemia hinge and the age and chest pain chain (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 242 training patients.
Resting blood pressure does not feed the score directly, so it acts only through the exertional ischaemia hinge, where it raises the risk in an uneven way.

Changing one input at a time across the whole model, more ST depression on exercise raises a typical patient's predicted risk in an uneven way, from about 13% at 0 mm to about 21% at 2.8 mm, the same as through the sum alone, where it rises steadily.
Across the whole model, compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina and non-anginal chest pain each lower it to about 3%.

hypothesis.text: The model adds up its inputs into one score: the vessels coloured (each extra vessel adding about the same), the ST segment, sex and chest pain type each move the predicted risk on their own, one part adds ST depression and resting blood pressure in an uneven way for patients whose ST segment does not slope up, a second acts on 132 of 242 training patients through age and chest pain, and the resting ECG is ignored.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results) the model predicts a risk of heart disease of about 15%; it adds up most of its inputs independently, one part adds ST depression and resting blood pressure in an uneven way for patients whose ST segment does not slope up, and a second part acts on 132 of 242 training patients through age, chest pain type and chest pain on exercise.

summary.label: Lowering the risk
summary.text: These add up independently, and these lower the risk: being a woman takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 15% to about 1% and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 4%; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 20% at 118 to about 13% at 175 beats per minute; and through this sum alone, compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina or non-anginal chest pain lowers it to about 2% and atypical angina to about 7%, and chest pain brought on by exercise lowers it to about 11%.

summary.label: Raising the risk
summary.text: Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 15% at 0 to about 95% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher; a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises it to about 41%, and higher cholesterol raises it steadily, from about 8% at 193 mg/dL to about 34% at 308 mg/dL.

Through this sum alone, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 55%, and more ST depression on exercise (from about 13% at 0 mm to about 21% at 2.8 mm) and older age (from about 11% at 42 to about 19% at 66 years) raise it steadily; chest pain type, chest pain on exercise, the ST segment, ST depression and age also act through the parts below.

summary.label: Rare results
summary.text: Some rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 and 17): a thallium result coded 4 raises the risk to about 95%, and through this sum alone a downsloping ST segment lowers it to about 13%; the model ignores the resting ECG.

This part reads chest pain type, resting blood pressure, chest pain on exercise, ST depression on exercise and the slope of the ST segment; for the typical patient, whose ST segment slopes up, it changes little: through it, typical angina and chest pain on exercise each leave the predicted risk at about 15%.

Its effect shows for patients whose ST segment does not slope up: across the whole model, more ST depression raises their risk in an uneven way, from about 51% at 0 mm to about 85% at 2.8 mm, against about 13% to about 21% with an upsloping ST segment.
Higher resting blood pressure raises the risk in an uneven way only for them, from about 55% at 110 mm Hg to about 77% at 155 mm Hg, while with an upsloping ST segment it stays at about 15%.
More ST depression also counts more without typical angina (from about 13% to about 21%, against about 2% to about 4% with it), rising in an uneven way.

This part reads age, chest pain type and chest pain on exercise and acts on 132 of 242 training patients, 83 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 99% without it and about 98% with it.

Through it, older age changes nothing until about 60 years (between 54 and 60 years for different patients), then lowers the predicted risk steadily: for a typical patient from about 17% at 42 to about 8% at 66 years.
Across the whole model, older age raises the risk steadily when exercise brings on chest pain (from about 9% to about 16%), but lowers it when it does not (from about 12% to about 10%).
Through it, any chest pain type other than no chest pain symptoms raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 15% to about 24%, and chest pain on exercise to about 18%.

parts.original_hypothesis: ROOT: HEART-DISEASE LOGIT. p = sigmoid(z) (get_formula prints ReLU at the output, but the model applies a sigmoid for this binary task). z = -0.796 + LINEAR CORE + 1.300*855 + 0.814*1501 - 0.515*3353, an additive composition. (1) LINEAR CORE: 16 direct input edges; largest weights ca +2.09, sex:1 +1.42, cp:4 +1.21, slope:2 +1.06, chol +0.76, thal:7 +0.66, cp:2 +0.58, fbs:0 +0.52, thal:4 +0.42; small negative terms exang:1 -0.33, thalach -0.20, exang:0 -0.15. Logit SD 3.94. (2) exertional_ischaemia_hinge (855/1501): a hinge on an ischaemia score (trestbps, oldpeak, exang:1 up; cp:1, slope:1 down) that is nearly flat below threshold and adds risk steeply above it (logit SD 1.64). A higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than an upsloping ST segment (in an uneven way for patients with slope of the ST segment at peak exercise other than an upsloping ST segment): for a typical patient, resting blood pressure going from 110 mm Hg to 155 mm Hg moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 55% to about 77% if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than an upsloping ST segment, and from about 15% to about 15% if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise.

A higher ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if chest pain type is something other than typical angina (in an uneven way for patients with chest pain type other than typical angina): for a typical patient, ST depression on exercise going from 0.0 mm to 2.8 mm moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 13% to about 21% if chest pain type is something other than typical angina, and from about 2% to about 4% if the patient has typical angina.
